text: Richard Stallman was born in New York City in 1953 to a Jewish family. He developed an early interest in computers and began programming at a young age. He attended the Harvard University and later MIT, where he worked on software projects like TECO and Emacs. Stallman became a prominent figure in the hacker community, criticizing restricted computer access and advocating for software freedom. In 1983, he announced the GNU project, a free operating system compatible with Unix, and founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF) to promote free software. He introduced the concept of copyleft and developed key tools like GNU Emacs, GCC, and GNU Debugger. Stallman argued that software should be free to use, study, and modify, and he opposed proprietary software and restrictive licensing. He promoted free software through activism, including protests against software patents and digital rights management, and advocated for reduced copyright. He emphasized the importance of terminology, insisting on "free software" over "open source" to highlight freedom. Stallman also promoted the use of GNU/Linux and criticized the term "Linux" as a misrepresentation. He has been involved in controversies, including criticism of his past writings on child pornography, which he later retracted. In 2019, he resigned from the FSF and MIT due to a controversy over his comments on Jeffrey Epstein. He later returned to the FSF board. Stallman lives in Boston and is known for his advocacy of software freedom and privacy, and he continues to promote free software through his work and public statements.
